transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s… it’s this thing with bridges. I know that may sound simple, but it’s gotten to where if I realize I have to cross one and there’s no way around it, the fear starts before I’m even on the bridge. My heart begins pounding, really pounding, and my hands get damp—on the steering wheel if I’m driving, or on the armrest if someone else is driving.

It’s that immediate rush of fear, just all at once, the moment the crossing feels unavoidable. I haven’t even reached the bridge yet and my body is already reacting like something terrible is about to happen. That’s what brought me in.
Is this intense fear or panic something you only experience with bridges, or does it happen in other situations as well?

It’s really bridges, doctor. I mean, I don’t get that same feeling just going about my day, at least not in that particular way. It’s when there’s a bridge involved—especially one of those high spans, or when I see on the map that the route is going to take me over one.

And the strange part is, I’m not confused about it. I know perfectly well that thousands and thousands of cars cross those bridges every day without anything happening. I can tell myself that. I do tell myself that. But when I see it ahead through the windshield, or even just realize it’s coming up, it’s as if my mind stops believing the ordinary facts. It feels like the whole structure is just waiting to drop away underneath us. Like the road won’t hold, even though I know that doesn’t make sense.

So no, it’s not a general thing with every situation. It’s very tied to bridges—seeing them, approaching them, knowing I have to cross them.
